lines.text: It's [8:55|eight fifty-five] on a Monday.
Your inbox is full, your calendar has three clashes,
and someone wants last quarter's number checked against the [CRM|C R M] before nine.
None of that is hard.
It's just busywork spread across five different apps.
What if you could hand it over in plain language, watch it get done, and stay in charge the whole time?
That's UiPath Delegate: a digital sidekick that learns from you and does real work across your apps.
In the next ten minutes I'll show you what it does, how it works, and how you keep control.
Delegate is a general-purpose agent with computer use.
You ask for something in plain language,
and it works across your browser and your applications to get it done.
You can start four ways: type a prompt, speak a command, record your screen, or start from a template.
Four ideas sit behind it.
First, offload the busywork: the repetitive admin that drains your time and focus.
Second, done, not suggested: it goes beyond advice and completes the task end to end.
Third, it's trainable, with skills that grow with how you work.
And fourth, it's enterprise-ready: programmatic execution, built to be reliable and secure.
AI can remove busywork, but only if it knows how to work inside the enterprise.
That's the gap Delegate is built for.
Let me show you the loop, because it's simple and it's the same every time.
One: you ask. In plain language, in a session.
No code, no [flowchart|flow chart].
Two: Delegate plans.
It works out the steps and which tools it needs, breaking a complex workflow into pieces.
Three: it acts, and it shows you.
Every action is visible as it happens.
If it's heading the wrong way, you can interrupt, correct, or redirect at any point.
Delegate also learns from your feedback over time.
Four: it stops when it should.
Anything that changes data, sends a message, or reaches into a sensitive system waits for your confirmation,
depending on your execution mode and what your organization allows.
I'll come back to that, because it's the part that makes this safe to use at work.
Under the hood it handles UI automation, files, and API calls,
and you can attach your own [SOPs|S O Ps] and product design documents so it works from your context, not a guess.
Now let's see it work.
The first thing Delegate is good at is tasks that cross systems.
Here I ask it to pull a figure from a report and check the related [CRM|C R M] record.
It doesn't stop after step one.
It handles the whole chain, so I get one complete answer without piecing the story together myself.
Next, the morning routine.
I ask it to triage my email and calendar first thing.
It reads both, and tells me what needs me and what can wait.
And once the rest is done, I ask it to draft a follow-up message.
It writes the draft using what it just found.
I review it, adjust the tone, and only then does anything get sent.
This pattern shows up across roles.
In our support example, a Product Support Engineer starts the day with one prompt:
pull my case backlog from Salesforce and prioritize the day.
Later they summarize the case in front of them, look up licensing data, and draft a first response,
all from one conversational surface, without switching tools.
Some work can't be automated the usual way.
The system has no usable API, and building a full automation would cost more than the task is worth.
For that, you teach Delegate by showing it.
Record yourself doing the task once.
Delegate turns that recording into a routine, or a knowledge skill, that it can repeat on your behalf.
That's the idea behind a trainable sidekick: you capture your expertise as a reusable playbook,
document a workflow once, and invoke it whenever you need it.
And skills aren't stuck with one person.
You can share them across the team, so everyone works the same way,
and nobody rebuilds what a colleague already taught it.
Here's where the hours disappear: turning raw data into something you can send.
Point Delegate at a spreadsheet, a database export, or a folder of files,
and ask for a presentation, a proposal, or a report.
It pulls the relevant data, structures it, and applies your formatting.
What used to take hours takes minutes,
and you're editing a finished draft instead of staring at a blank slide.
The same idea powers some of the bigger enterprise use cases:
generating process and solution design documents, running application test cases,
and taking intake and triage off a clerical team's plate.
Chat is great, but sometimes you need the real thing, a proper form or a table you can actually work in.
When Delegate connects to a system that provides its own interface,
it can show that system's real screens inside the conversation.
Lists, forms, tables, and dashboards render inline, not as a description of them.
Forms arrive already filled in with sensible values,
so you change only what matters instead of describing every field in chat.
You keep the precision of the real interface without leaving the conversation.
This works through [MCP|M C P] Apps.
Everything I've shown you so far has one more trick.
When a session goes well, you don't have to do it again.
Save any successful Delegate session as a reusable routine.
Build it once, say a weekly sales pipeline report, or a monthly expense categorization,
and from then on you can run it on demand with a single click, or schedule it to run automatically.
You invest the time once to teach Delegate a workflow, then you benefit every time after that.
And it isn't just for you.
You can share a routine with your team, so each person isn't rebuilding the same thing from scratch.
Of course, the question everyone asks is: how much do I trust it?
You decide, with three approval modes.
Cautious asks before every operation.
It's the safest, with the most approval prompts.
Adaptive auto-approves known safe operations, and it's the recommended setting.
Full access has no approval prompts at all, so keep it for trusted environments only.
Inside Adaptive there's a Smart approvals toggle.
Turn it on and Delegate also approves what the model judges safe.
You get the fewest prompts, but the model can misjudge, so that's a trade-off you choose on purpose.
You can also set allow and deny lists for apps and URLs, and granular permissions by task type.
Every action lands in an audit trail, and your data stays in your control.
Because Delegate ships on the UiPath platform, every operation inherits controls you already run:
Orchestrator for scheduling and run management,
a credential vault so secrets are never exposed to the agent,
the AI Trust Layer for policy and redaction,
and role-based access mapped to your organization.
Not bolted on. Built in.
Let's recap.
Delegate completes tasks that cross applications.
It learns repetitive work from a recording.
It turns raw data into a finished deliverable.
It works through a system's own screens.
And it saves what works as routines you can reuse and share, all under approval modes you control.
Delegate the busywork. Keep the judgment.
If you're already on UiPath, Delegate ships as an extension of what you have.
The UiPath Assistant upgrades into it, with no new IT approval and no new upgrade process.
The getting-started guide and the product page are linked below.
Open a session, ask for one small thing, and meet your first [AI-intern|AI intern].
